items.originalTitle: ‘A savagely brutal map’: Senate GOP braces for 2028
items.author: Meredith Lee Hill
items.title: ‘A savagely brutal map’: Senate GOP braces for 2028
items.summary: Sen. Bernie Moreno isn’t sugarcoating things. The incoming chair of the National Republican Senatorial Committee will be in charge of defending 19 GOP seats in 2028 — and he’ll need to flip at least six more to regain control of the Senate majority. “Looking at it right now, it's absolutely a savagely brutal map,” the Ohio Republican said in an interview on Capitol Hill. After a historic midterms shellacking, Moreno is in the hot seat as he looks to navigate his chamber — and the party — through a rebuilding of its brand and its base over next two years. Republicans will likely have just 44 seats heading into 2028. They need to hold onto seats in battleground states like Wisconsin and North Carolina, while trying to flip seats held by Democratic Sens. Mark Kelly in Arizona, John Fetterman in Pennsylvania, Raphael Warnock in Georgia and Catherine Cortez Masto in Nevada. Moreno and his team have interviewed a handful of candidates over the last few days to be the next NRSC executive director, according to four people with direct knowledge of the matter, granted anonymity to discuss private conversations. Republicans expect Chris Grant, a former Moreno and Trump campaign staffer who now runs his own firm, to serve as a main outside GOP consultant for the committee. On top of the grueling map ahead, the Ohio Republican is facing the additional task of working with a lame duck president who still wields immense power over the GOP and its primaries. Then there’s the vice president, who is likely to run for president himself in the same two-year sprint. Moreno is close with both of those men. Asked how involved he expects the White House to be in GOP primaries and recruiting going forward, he replied, “We’re going to work on all of that.” It’ll be a complicated path forward. Moreno, over the past cycle has been unwilling to cast blame on President Donald Trump or Vice President JD Vance. Days before the midterm elections, he said if Republicans lost, it would be because people were “pissed off” about high gas prices. He’s unlikely to completely distance himself and the NRSC brand from the president's influence. But the party is currently undergoing a reckoning of how closely to align with the president after voters delivered an uncompromising rebuke of Trump’s economic agenda. Across the country, several battlegrounds and once-thought-to-be-safe red territory fell to Democratic hands. Trump in the 2026 cycle angered many Senate Republicans by supporting a primary challenge against Sen. John Cornyn of Texas — a move they privately say cost them north of $200 million as they tried, in vain, to save Ken Paxton’s imperiled campaign. The president also supported a primary challenge against Sen. Bill Cassidy of Louisiana, and pushed Sen. Thom Tillis to decide to retire in highly competitive North Carolina. One of the biggest challenges before Moreno and Senate Republicans after the midterms wipeout is to find candidates who can win a general election in highly competitive states, while also making it through GOP primaries where Trump will be a major factor. They’ll need to push back on the White House if the president tries, once again, to intervene — though that’s easier said than done. “There will be no patience for bad recruits this cycle,” said one senior Republican granted anonymity to discuss internal conversations, referring to the implosions of Paxton, Michael Whatley in North Carolina and other Republicans who were hand-picked by Trump. The White House referred POLITICO to Trump's post-midterms comments, where he blamed his party’s losses on the fact that he wasn’t on the ballot and said he brought several candidates "closer to victory," though they ultimately lost. Senate Majority Leader John Thune — who will be the minority leader next year — and his team plan to be heavily involved in recruitment efforts, according to two people involved in the conversations, granted anonymity to speak candidly. Their goal, one of the people said, is “to make sure we have our strongest possible candidates on the ballot in 2028.” Moreno is already trying to find a GOP recruit in his home state of Ohio to run against incoming Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown, whose term will be up again in 2028 after he won a special election against GOP Sen. Jon Husted earlier this month. The new NRSC chair said he’s looking for “somebody who can beat the crap out of Sherrod Brown.” Husted in private conversations hasn’t completely ruled out another bid, but he’s indicated he’s unlikely to run again, according to three people with knowledge of the matter, granted anonymity to speak candidly. Ohio Republicans expect former state Sen. Kevin Coughlin to explore a potential Senate bid. And they’re watching Rep. Mike Turner (R-Ohio), who just lost his reelection. Husted did not respond to a request for comment. Turner spokesperson Frank DeBrosse said in a statement that the representative "has been approached by several people about this and is keeping all his options open.” If Vance doesn’t seek his own presidential bid, Republicans in his home state are holding a long-shot hope that he, too, might consider a return to his old job. “JD Vance would be a dream candidate,” said one Ohio Republican. A version of this article first appeared in POLITICO Pro’s Morning Score . Want to receive the newsletter every weekday? Subscribe to POLITICO Pro . You’ll also receive daily policy news and other intelligence you need to act on the day’s biggest stories.

items.originalTitle: Poll: Less than a third of Americans expect the next president to be Republican
items.author: Jason Beeferman
items.title: Poll: Less than a third of Americans expect the next president to be Republican
items.summary: Nearly twice as many Americans expect a Democrat to win the presidency in 2028 than they do a Republican, a new POLITICO Poll finds . Even one in five of President Donald Trump’s own 2024 voters believe Republicans will lose the White House, a bad sign for the GOP as it struggles to recover from widespread losses this cycle and figure out its identity after spending a decade orbiting around Trump. Just 60% of Trump voters believe Republicans will keep the White House. Democratic voters are far more confident about their own party, according to the survey conducted by PF Global in the days after the midterm: Among voters who backed Kamala Harris, 87% expect Democrats to win in 2028. Beneath the unity is disagreement over what kind of nominee to pick. Pluralities of voters agree the next president should be a fighter when asked to choose from a list of qualities. But voters across the ideological spectrum also said they want other things from the country’s 48th president. While 43% of Harris voters want “a fighter,” 40% also selected “a progressive” and 34% chose “creative.” Among Trump voters, the 45% said they want to see “a conservative” elected president, surpassing the 39% who picked “a fighter.” They're also divided over what background their nominees should come from. Nearly three in 10 Trump voters say they would prefer the next president be someone who has not worked in Trump’s administration. That number rises to 46% among Trump voters who don’t identify as MAGA, whereas 82% of his loyal MAGA base would prefer the next president be someone who did work for Trump. That debate is playing out in real-time among top GOP leaders and lawmakers. More and more Hill Republicans are eyeing Secretary of State Marco Rubio for 2028, who they say is less associated with the midterm bloodbath than Vice President JD Vance. Others say the nominee should be someone entirely outside of Trump’s direct orbit. “As much as I like Rubio, and as much as I like Vance, they can't be our nominee,” said Dan McMaster, the chair of Michigan’s Shiawassee County Republican Party. “We need to get a Republican as far away from Trump as possible, and even then, I think it's going to be a battle.” “You've got to have some fresh blood in there, and you've got to have someone that has some distance from the crap that's gone on the last two years,” said one GOP strategist who worked on multiple House races last cycle and was granted anonymity to speak candidly about their own party. In a statement, Natalie Baldassarre, a spokesperson for the Republican National Committee, said the president isn’t going anywhere. "President Trump remains the unequivocal leader of our party who's cut taxes, lowered drug costs, and secured our border,” Baldassarre said. “Republicans will continue to harness his ability to energize our base and expose the Democrats' disastrous record to win in 2028." The White House also pointed POLITICO to separate polling earlier this month that shows Trump’s approval rating sits at 75% with all Republicans and jumps to 93% with those who identify as MAGA. “President Trump will never stop delivering results for the American people and he will undoubtedly go down as the most successful and consequential president in American history,” said Davis Ingle, a White House spokesperson. On election night earlier this month, Trump blamed his party’s losses on the fact that he wasn’t on the ballot, telling POLITICO by phone , “I wasn't on the ballot. If I was on the ballot, we would have won; we would have won it all very easily.” Meanwhile, Democrats have their own disagreements to figure out as they select their nominee. This cycle’s blue wave has bolstered the progressive wing of the party, which has long hoped to prove their candidates can win in purple battlegrounds, not just in safe-blue states. But the poll reveals skepticism remains — at least among moderates — over whether progressive wins in 2026 can translate to the presidential stage in 2028. The survey found a majority of progressive Democrats — 63% — want a progressive to be president, compared with just 23% of moderates who say the same. Half of progressive Democrats are convinced that being a progressive is a quality that will get their candidate elected in 2028. Moderates are less certain of that, though they’re also not as confident in their own faction: Just 37% think being a moderate is a quality that ensures the Democratic candidate wins. “Whoever's running for president has seen what's happened and also has seen the power of our movement, and so this is something that could be carried on to 2028,” said progressive New Jersey Democratic Rep.-elect Adam Hamawy, reflecting on the wins he and others enjoyed this cycle. “Despite it being the most expensive elections in history, we showed that people are able to beat out money when we come together.” And with Democrats winning Senate seats in deep-red states like Kansas and Mississippi for the first time in decades, many now argue that the entire map is in play for 2028. The poll found that 60% of Democrats think the party should focus their efforts on winning all states in the presidential election, even ones that seemed like deep Republican areas, rather than focus on holding the states where they know their supporters are. Republicans felt the same, with 56% also arguing for an “all states” approach as the party races to rebuild in territory they once thought was safe. “I have been very, very loud about the fact that the path to the presidency leads through the South,” said Democratic strategist Dallas Jones, who ran statewide Black voter engagement for Lone Star Rising PAC, the outside group that supported Texas Sen.-elect James Talarico. “But again, we don't make investments there. We're playing the same electoral map with the same swing states.”

items.originalTitle: Mary Peltola unseats Sen. Dan Sullivan, giving Dems a 56-seat Senate majority
items.author: Lisa Kashinsky
items.title: Mary Peltola unseats Sen. Dan Sullivan, giving Dems a 56-seat Senate majority
items.summary: Former Rep. Mary Peltola ousted GOP Sen. Dan Sullivan in Alaska — the first time in 18 years a Democrat has won a Senate race in the state. Her win gives Democrats a 56-44 edge in the Senate. Peltola was one of Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer’s top recruits for the cycle. She overpowered a Republican rescue mission for Sullivan and allegations of misconduct against her from former staffers to flip a state President Donald Trump won by 13 points in 2024. Her victory continues the blue wave born from voters’ frustrations at high costs and the Trump administration. Peltola will return to Washington, where she will become the first Alaska Native to serve in the Senate after previously holding the same distinction in the House. Her campaign had projected confidence about her path to victory as the vote count dragged on in a far-flung, rural state with long grace periods for late-arriving ballots. But her win was not without tumult. Trump’s Department of Justice sued to try to stop the certification if Sullivan lost, claiming voters could be confused by his same-name challenger. The president went so far as to call for votes for retired teacher Dan J. Sullivan and another longshot candidate in the four-way, all-party contest to be transferred to the incumbent. The Justice Department also started probing efforts to recruit Dan J. Sullivan after a New York Times report suggesting members of Peltola’s campaign and Senate Democrats’ campaign arm were involved. Both had previously denied involvement.

items.originalTitle: Grand Theft Auto VI review – gaming’s most depraved world is now also its greatest love story
items.author: Keza MacDonald
items.title: Grand Theft Auto VI review – gaming’s most depraved world is now also its greatest love story
items.summary: With realism that defies belief, this vast game easily accommodates its trademark foulmouthed, OTT chaos – as well as new empathy for the fugitive couple at its centre In GTA VI, Rockstar has created the most extraordinarily, indulgently detailed virtual world that we have yet seen. Reviewing it feels a bit like trying to review, say, Paris: it contains so many potential experiences that it’s hard to know where to start. If you had been spying on me playing this game over the past few weeks you may well have caught me robbing banks, shooting up a weed farm or tearing along the highway at sunset blaring Bad Bunny on the in-game radio, but you might equally have caught me doing squats at the gym, shopping, assembling a coffee table or walking along the beach eating ice-cream. There is such a multiplicity of things on offer here that it is difficult to nail down what this game definitively is. Is it an interactive crime movie? A city simulator? A driving game? A sort of absurdly expansive version of The Sims in which the people you’re dressing up and looking after just happen to be professional criminals? It will be different for everyone – that is the beauty of it. For me, though, this game is about Jason and Lucia, the fugitive couple through whom you experience all that Leonida has to offer. Jason is muscular, handsome, ex-military, steady and unflappable, sincere but spare with words. Lucia has been boosting cars since the age of 14, has a wicked sense of humour and takes zero bullshit. (Lucia is the scarier one; I found myself turning much more quickly to violence when playing as her.) At the start, Lucia is incarcerated and Jason is making a go of things in the sunbeaten Keys, working for a dodgy guy down on the marina and renting a run-down house on stilts with a jetty round the back and a pet snake. When Lucia gets out of prison, the two of them try to make some kind of life for themselves – but before long they get caught up with the wrong people and have to flee the cosy life they’ve just started building.

items.originalTitle: Hakeem Jeffries on Track For Speaker Nomination in Wednesday Vote
items.author: Nik Popli
items.title: Hakeem Jeffries on Track For Speaker Nomination in Wednesday Vote
items.summary: Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, the House Minority Leader, speaks during a news conference at the Capitol Building in Washington, DC., on Nov. 12, 2026, after midterm elections in which Democrats won control of the House. —Anna Moneymaker—Getty Images When House Democrats gather Wednesday to choose their nominee for speaker, there will be little doubt about the outcome. Despite lingering divisions, Representative Hakeem Jeffries of New York is on course to become the first Black American to lead the chamber after steering his party to victory in this month's midterm elections. The vote will mark a milestone in Jeffries’ political career, four years after he succeeded Nancy Pelosi as the top House Democrat and more than a decade after he entered Congress. Now, he is preparing to lead a chamber where Democrats are projected to hold approximately 259 seats, a commanding majority that would give him considerably more room to maneuver than the narrow Republican majority that preceded it. Jeffries, 56, faces no declared challenger and needs only a simple majority of House Democrats to secure the nomination. His longtime deputies, Representatives Katherine Clark of Massachusetts and Pete Aguilar of California, are expected to become majority leader and majority whip, respectively, while Representative Ted Lieu of California is in line to become Democratic caucus chair. The full House will vote to formally elect its leaders when the new Congress convenes on Jan. 3. The transition from minority leader to Speaker would put Jeffries at the center of the political battles during the final two years of President Trump's term, giving Democrats control over the House's legislative agenda and investigative committees. His party has promised to use that authority to scrutinize the Trump Administration and demonstrate to voters that Democrats can govern ahead of the 2028 presidential election. But the breadth of the Democratic victory has also produced competing expectations about what the party should accomplish with its newfound power. Progressives, many of whom are not publicly backing Jeffries, are pressing for more ambitious legislation on health care, corporate power and military assistance to Israel, while moderates are emphasizing affordability and policies that could attract bipartisan support. The divisions are unlikely to threaten Jeffries's speakership, given the size of his majority, but they could shape the agenda he pursues and the political compromises he is willing to make. Read more : In Hakeem Jeffries’ Rise to Speaker, Black Leaders See a Milestone—and a Test Leading up to Wednesday’s vote, an unusually intense campaign unfolded behind the scenes to present a united front. In recent days, Jeffries and his allies have been working to secure an overwhelming show of support, soliciting endorsements from major Democratic factions and meeting privately with lawmakers who have expressed reservations about his leadership. Jeffries was scheduled to meet Tuesday with leaders of the Congressional Progressive Caucus, the New Democrat Coalition and the Blue Dog Coalition, part of an effort to hear concerns from across the party before the vote. Some of his supporters initially favored nominating him by acclamation, a display of unanimity that would have avoided a formal tally. But Jeffries instead said Tuesday that he would call for a recorded secret ballot, allowing Democrats to register their positions privately before the public speaker election in January. Under Democratic caucus rules, leadership elections are conducted by secret ballot unless members agree to waive that requirement. Wednesday's vote will disclose the overall tally but not how individual lawmakers voted. Members will cast their ballots through an application on their House-issued phones. Progressives, emboldened by a series of primary victories and the arrival of several democratic socialists, have pressed Jeffries to promise a committee markup next year on Medicare for All legislation and bring forward the Block the Bombs Act, which would restrict certain offensive weapons transfers to Israel. Jeffries has not publicly committed to any such moves, and has appeared largely untroubled by the prospect of defections, pointing to his party's electoral performance and expressing confidence that he has secured enough support. "You think I don't have the votes nailed down?" he asked a reporter last week, smiling. Jeffries’ path to the gavel Taking the Speaker’s gavel would mark the culmination of a political rise centered in Brooklyn, where Jeffries grew up as the son of an Air Force veteran and a social worker. He often talks about how the devastation of the crack epidemic during the 1980s shaped his interest in public service and his desire to improve conditions for working-class families who remained in struggling neighborhoods. Read more : Jeffries' Fraternity Days Set Stage For His Career After attending the State University of New York at Binghamton, Georgetown University and New York University School of Law, Jeffries worked as a corporate lawyer before turning to politics. He lost his first two campaigns for the New York State Assembly, but he eventually won a seat in the Legislature. In 2012, he challenged a longtime Democratic congressman who withdrew from the race, clearing a path for his election to the House. In Congress, Jeffries has developed a reputation as a disciplined political communicator and coalition builder, cultivating relationships across the party's ideological spectrum as he rose through its leadership ranks. When Pelosi stepped aside after the 2022 elections, he succeeded her as the top House Democrat, becoming the first Black lawmaker to lead either party in Congress. His election as speaker would carry a historic significance beyond his own career, placing a Black American for the first time in an office second in the line of presidential succession, after the Vice President. It would also come more than 150 years after Joseph Rainey of South Carolina became the first Black member of the House during Reconstruction. Pushback from progressives Democrats have promised to use their control of Congress to pursue an ambitious legislative agenda and subject the Trump Administration to the kind of scrutiny that Republican leaders have largely resisted. The House's investigative committees would be able to examine allegations of corruption and abuses of executive authority, as well as the administration's handling of the war in Iran. Some Democrats are openly discussing impeachment proceedings against senior administration officials, including Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. But their ability to enact legislation will remain constrained by Trump's veto power and the Senate's 60-vote threshold for advancing most bills. Those obstacles have helped fuel a debate over whether the party should concentrate on legislation that might attract Republican support or pursue more ambitious measures that could establish its priorities for the 2028 election. Jeffries has sought to leave room for both approaches, outlining an agenda organized around affordability and accountability. His immediate priorities include restoring enhanced Affordable Care Act tax credits that expired earlier this year, reversing Republican Medicaid spending cuts, and repealing tariffs imposed by the Trump Administration. In recent weeks, progressives have flooded congressional offices with calls and emails urging lawmakers to oppose Jeffries. Some regard him as an embodiment of a Democratic establishment they believe has been too cautious in confronting Trump and too accommodating of corporate interests. At a Democratic conference in Denver last weekend, protesters repeatedly interrupted Jeffries with demands for Medicaid for All, a Green New Deal, and an embargo on American weapons transfers to Israel. Similar frustrations in the Senate have prompted Senator Chris Van Hollen of Maryland to challenge Senator Chuck Schumer of New York, the current minority leader, for the job of majority leader in the new Congress. Though Schumer appears likely to retain his leadership post, Senate Democrats aren’t expected to settle that contest until next month. Unlike in the Senate, opposition in the lower chamber never coalesced around another candidate. Representative Jamie Raskin of Maryland, whose name has circulated as a possible alternative, has ruled out a bid as he’s in line to chair the powerful House Judiciary Committee. Representative Ayanna Pressley of Massachusetts, the subject of an online effort to draft her, has also made clear that she did not intend to run. "I do not need to be the speaker of the House to speak for the people," Pressley told constituents at a town hall on Monday. Medicare for All Less than 24 hours before the nomination vote, Jeffries held a news conference and laid out more of his legislative vision. He embraced proposals to lower the Medicare eligibility age, expand coverage to include dental, vision and hearing benefits, and guarantee health coverage for children. "Those are bold actions, meaningful actions, important actions that can be taken on our march toward universal health coverage," Jeffries told reporters. The proposals drew praise from Senator Bernie Sanders of Vermont, the leading proponent of Medicare for All, who said they resembled the first stage of his plan to move the country toward a single-payer system. But Jeffries has stopped short of endorsing Medicare for All itself, a distinction that illustrates the policy disagreements he will encounter even on an issue that Democrats have identified as a central priority. The Congressional Progressive Caucus is expected to grow to more than 100 members in the next Congress, while the New Democrat Coalition, the largest ideological faction in the House Democratic Caucus, will number more than 140. Both groups support expanding access to health care and reversing Republican cuts, but they differ over whether Democrats should seek to replace the existing insurance system. The New Democrats have expressed skepticism about Medicare for All, arguing that competition among private insurers can help control costs. Progressives are also seeking more aggressive action on corporate power, campaign finance, and American military assistance to Israel, among other issues. Their growing ranks could give them substantial influence over the House agenda, even if their efforts to challenge Jeffries's leadership have gained little traction. The political circumstances are almost the reverse of those confronting Pelosi when Democrats last reclaimed the House during a Trump presidency. In 2018, it was moderate Democrats who objected to her return as speaker, arguing that the party needed new leadership after years under her command. Pelosi ultimately overcame the resistance and went on to wield considerable authority over Trump's first term, overseeing major investigations and two impeachments of the President. Jeffries now faces skepticism primarily from the left, though he approaches the speakership with a larger majority and without the organized challenge that confronted his predecessor. His political strength will likely make Wednesday's election a relatively straightforward affair, but it remains uncertain how he will exercise that authority. Representative-elect Don Leonard of Ohio said in a video posted to social media last week that senior Democrats had warned him they would make his life a "living hell" if he refused to support Jeffries. Leonard later met with the Democratic leader to discuss his concerns. At Tuesday’s news conference, Jeffries adopted a welcoming tone toward the incoming lawmakers. "It's a great class, and they have a lot of wonderful ideas—fresh ideas, new ideas—about how to advance the ball in a bold way for the American people," Jeffries said. "I embrace those conversations."

items.originalTitle: Irish Man Charged With Destroying U.S. Military Plane Becomes Protest Symbol
items.author: Miranda Jeyaretnam
items.title: Irish Man Charged With Destroying U.S. Military Plane Becomes Protest Symbol
items.summary: Protesters outside Shannon Airport, Co Clare, where President Donald Trump will depart from at the end of his trip to the Republic of Ireland, on Sept. 13, 2026. —Clodagh Kilcoyne—PA Images/Getty Images An Irish man has been charged in the U.S. with wielding an axe and using chemicals to destroy an American military plane in what supporters have described as a protest against the U.S. military. Federal prosecutors in Manhattan accused 48-year-old Daithí O’Corrain of damaging a $60 million U.S. Air National Guard aircraft while it was parked at Ireland’s Shannon airport in April. O’Corrain allegedly cut hydraulic lines, smashed cockpit gauges, and poured ball bearings into the fuel tanks of the plane, according to an indictment unsealed on Tuesday. O’Corrain is not in U.S. custody and his arraignment has not been scheduled. He was arrested by Irish police after the April 11 incident. He faces one charge in the U.S. of destruction of government property, and three charges in Ireland of trespassing, causing criminal damage to the perimeter fence at the airport, and causing criminal damage to the plane. If convicted, the U.S. charge carries a maximum sentence of 10 years in prison. “These charges send a clear and powerful message that attacks on U.S. military assets—and thus our national security—will not be tolerated,” U.S. Attorney Jamie McDonald said in a statement . A group of public supporters has rallied around O’Corrain, characterizing his actions as a political protest against the U.S. war with Iran and military aid to Israel. An online fundraiser described him as an “independent peace activist” and called the incident “an inspiring act of direct action … to resist the unwanted presence of the U.S. Military in Ireland.” Anti-nuclear, anti-war newspaper The Nuclear Resister reported in August that activists attended his court hearings in Ireland. Social media accounts made in support of O’Corrain posted information about solidarity protests and argued that the aircraft’s presence violated Irish rules governing foreign military aircraft. The Irish government has said that U.S. military aircraft landing in Ireland are subject to conditions, including restrictions on carrying arms without permission, and that missions aren’t launched from the airport. O’Corrain has not made any public statements and is not known to be involved in any activist groups behind earlier protests at the airport, including when President Donald Trump visited in September. Here’s what to know about the charges. Prosecutors say O’Corrain planned for months According to the indictment, O’Corrain breached the airport’s security perimeter at around 4:39 a.m. local time and entered the aircraft by breaking its rear crew door’s locking mechanism. He then covered the plane’s windows, except those in the cockpit, barricaded himself inside, and placed ball bearings mixed with epoxy into the plane door tracks to block them from being opened, the indictment alleges. O’Corrain is alleged to have cut wire bundles and hydraulic lines, crimped a liquid oxygen line, destroyed the gauges in the cockpit, and punctured the plane’s air ducts. At around 9:40 a.m., the flight crew saw O’Corrain escaping out of a roof hatch before striking the plane with an axe and pouring unknown substances and ball bearings into the plane’s fuel tanks, according to the indictment. Handout photo of items allegedly used by Irish national Daithi O'Corrain to barricade himself in a U.S. military aircraft, distributed on Nov. 17, 2026. —U.S. Department of Justice/Press Association/AP Prosecutors alleged that O’Corrain had planned for months to break into the airport and damage the aircraft, including searching online about the construction of the C-130 Hercules aircraft and for coordinates for where to breach the airport’s security perimeter. The plane, a quad-engine turboprop that is mainly used for military transport, was parked on the airport’s taxiway while en route to a military assignment in another country. Prosecutors also alleged that O’Corrain ordered capsules of a corrosive chemical, gallium, online, subscribed to a flight-tracker app, and attempted to contact a person who had been arrested in connection with a prior breach at the airport. He demonstrated “detailed knowledge” of the layout of the aircraft and how to destroy its critical components without compromising his safety, the indictment said, adding that he knew in advance the aircraft would be there. “This was not an act of spontaneous vandalism,” said James Barnacle, head of the FBI’s New York office. Anti-war protests at Shannon Airport Shannon Airport has been the site of multiple protests against what critics describe as Ireland’s role in allowing U.S. military flights and troop transport through the airport. Protesters have argued that the U.S.’s involvement in various wars, particularly ongoing ones in Iran and Gaza, conflicts with Irish military neutrality. According to Gaza’s Health Ministry, Israel has killed more than 74,000 people in Gaza since the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas attack on southern Israel, which killed around 1,200 people in Israel and saw about 250 others taken hostage. In the absence of independent monitoring on the ground, the ministry is the primary source for casualty data relied upon by humanitarian groups, journalists, and international bodies. Its figures do not differentiate between civilians and combatants and cannot be independently verified by TIME. An investigation by The Guardian estimated that 83% of Palestinians killed in Gaza were civilians as of May 2025, citing data from the Israel Defense Forces. In April 2017, Dan Dowling, then 35, and Edward Horgan, then 71, entered a restricted area and wrote “Danger, danger, do not fly” in red marker on a U.S. Navy aircraft. They were arrested in Ireland, and the jury heard in court that the markings were wiped off before the plane flew onward to a U.S. base in the Middle East. “If you want my motivation, it is the killing of children in Iraq, Syria, Afghanistan and Yemen,” Horgan told reporters at the time, calling their action an “informative protest” to highlight that U.S. military aircraft were not being searched. He said he had handed Irish police at the airport a 35-page-long list of 1,000 children killed in conflicts involving the U.S. in the Middle East, Asia, and Africa. Both men were acquitted of criminal damage in 2023, but convicted of trespass. Earlier this month, Ireland’s Supreme Court overturned Dowling’s trespass conviction. His attorney argued that the men believed their actions were necessary to protect lives. On March 10, 2024, pro-Palestinian activists held a sit-in inside the terminal calling for an end to U.S. weapons transfers through Ireland. Later that month, three pro-Palestinian activists approached a U.S. military aircraft carrying a Palestinian flag and a banner that read, “U.S. military out of Shannon.” They sat near the plane in an attempt to stop it from taking off. The activists were arrested and charged . Their trial was adjourned in February pending the Supreme Court ruling in Dowling’s appeal. Galway Palestine Solidarity Campaign organizer Rania Muhareb told Irish newspaper The Journal that the activists were protesting “in line with a long tradition of Irish anti-war activism at Shannon.” Around 500 people held another protest in support of Palestinians in April 2024 at the airport entrance, while a smaller group blocked the access road. In May 2025, three people were arrested for driving a van through the airport’s perimeter fence in what was reported as a pro-Palestinian protest. In a separate incident that month, three women allegedly entered the runway and spray-painted the nose of a plane of Omni Air, a civilian airline that transports U.S. military personnel. Irish broadcaster RTÉ reported that the plane was not engaged in military activity. The women were arrested and charged with criminal damage and trespass, which they denied. That November, three people were charged over allegedly entering the airfield and spray-painting a U.S. Navy Reserve Boeing 737 parked at Shannon. Their stated objection was that U.S. military use of Shannon violated Irish neutrality and supported Israel’s war in Gaza. Hundreds of protesters also gathered near Shannon Airport during President Donald Trump’s visit to Ireland in September, chanting “U.S. military out of Shannon.”
